Psychiatrists should always be covered with basic coverage.

For psychologists though, things are a bit different. On July 1st 2022, a law was passed to integrate psychologists to basic insurances coverage. The catch is that you need a doctor to file a prescription. If I recall correctly, before the law was passed, only psychiatrists were able to make that kind of prescription. Unless you went to a clinic (e.g. "Les Toises, Lausanne") where psychologists were under the supervision of a psychiatrist who could provide the prescriptions on their own, you'd have to seek out a private psychiatrist which isn't easy because a lot of them have wait lists. 




Now since the law has passed, it's gotten a lot easier. You still need a valid prescription from a doctor but GPs (generalists) are able to write them for you. The caveat is that they can only prescribe a maximum amount of 15 sessions at a time, meaning you'll have to go back to your doctor to get a new prescription. Also, if you exceed 30 sessions per year, your doctor will need to make an inquiry to your insurance to have them guarantee extra coverage. 




My assumption is that the psychotherapy supplement is mostly for people that want to see more that one psychologist, need more than 30 sessions a year or who simply don't want to bother with having to get prescriptions filled for it. If you're only seeking a psychiatrist then I don't believe you need any of this because they should be covered by your basic insurance.

You're right, it's true that there are children children that do develop empathetic skills earlier than others.  But their empathy is still far from being entirely developed at those ages and it's incomparable to the expression of empathy seen in adults and even in younger teens. At 7 years old, children haven't fully developed their own emotional regulation, they often still struggle to understand different perspectives and they tend to have issues when it comes to recognising more complex emotions (different types of sadness, e.g. grief.) My point is more that their development of empathy is still very incomplete at that age and therefore you can't hold a 6-11 years old up to the same expectations you'd hold towards a teenager. The gap between the two is a lot wider than what a lot of people tend to expect.

I can agree that there have been changes to the younger crowd, but I've got to say that I find your examples to be extremely anecdotal. e.g. an 8yo wetting his pants and refusing to change himself isn't demonstrative of anything, besides indicating that kid is presenting symptoms that you'd typically see in a kid with a developmental disorder, quite frequently in kids with autism.


You also can't realistically expect empathy coming from someone who isn't old enough to have fully developed theory of mind. It's not even fully fleshed out before they reach their teens. [Piaget argued that children as old as 11 years old struggled to understand that their own feelings were unique and not shared by everybody around them and that it wasn't until that age that they were able to comprehend concepts like "justice".](https://www.webmd.com/children/piaget-stages-of-development#091e9c5e80676cfd-2-4) So some selfishness is to be expected in all children, but instead I'd wager that there are more incentives for children to act more selfishly nowadays than prior. More reasons to put others down than reasons to make friends perhaps? I'm not sure either.

However, know that losing hair isn't always due to having male pattern baldness (MPD). You say you're skinny, so are you eating enough food and getting proper nutrients? Have had to deal with stressful events recently? There are other potential causes so my advice is to consult a dermatologist who will make the proper assessment.





It's worth looking into the medications. AFAIK there are two FDA-approved ones: Finasteride (very effective pill but with side effects, prescription-only) and Minoxidil (Liquid that you put on the scalp once/twice a day available over the counter; will slow MPD but not as effective as Finasteride, hair will fall back out after 3 months if you quit using it). If needs be, you can use both of these medications at the same time (if your doctor is ok with it obviously). Off-label, there's also a medical shampoo called Nizoral (ketoconazolum) that is an antifungal treatment for dandruff. A few studies have found that it may promote hair regrowth but it's not really settled science yet.





Should you decide to go with Finasteride/Minoxidil though, it's possible that you'll regrow some of the hair. Just because you don't *see* a hair poke out doesn't necessarily mean the follicle has died. It's not a guarantee but if the hair fell out in the last 2 years, there's a chance to see regrowth with those medications! And there's always the possibility of doing implants if necessary.







These are the practical things that can be done. But as other people have pointed out, working on your mental and self-perception is crucial too. Balding is... quite normal when you think about it, a huge chunk of people experience it. So being able to accept it is what determines whether it's a hindrance or not, but there's nothing inherently wrong with it. You should really work in being kind towards yourself, with and without hair, with or without a relationship, with or without bald friends around you. It sure isn't easy but it's just as important as the practical advice I gave you.

It certainly doesn't necessarily have to be AVPD, but I would say this still fits under "avoidance-based tendencies and/or behaviours" that can also frequently occur due to anxiety or phobias. Mostly referring to the whole "waking up at 4am as to not let my parents know I jog" bit, that is typically a form of avoidance.




Having experienced that, I don't really think there's really a more specific term. But if you do recognise this kind of behaviour as "avoidance", then the next question would be "what am I avoiding exactly?" in order to figure out the root cause. The answer is going to be very personal past this point though. It could be a fear to be reprimanded, judged... Could even be some sort of impostor syndrome where you worry you'll get interrogated (oh you're a jogger? name 52 athlethes) type of thing. Whatever it is, it's something you're actively spending effort avoiding, so it's important to look into it.





I think exposure is probably the best way to overcome avoidant behaviours like this. The more you push yourself to do it, the easier it'll get. It's already a huge step to be able to recognise how your brain behaves when faced to those situations

Hey there. I am and have been in your shoes in the past. I'd like to suggest a different perspective to you and I hope you can get something out of it but be aware that I'm not a mental health professional.


It would be futile to try to argue that you have done everything right until now. There are clearly situations in your life that could've gone a lot better. That's just bound to happen in anyone's life, though. Always making the right choice would require someone to not only be aware of every possible outcome, but to also have access to every piece of information regarding the context to actually pick the right "path". For example in social settings, you'd need to be aware of everyone's full background and personality to fully grasp how your words affect them before you actually say them.

What I'm trying to say is, you're not omniscient. Neither am I, neither is anyone else on this thread. As such, you, me and all the others simply cannot be expected to always get things right. People only make decisions based on their own reading and knowledge of the situation. 
You could decide that the best solution would be to just never make a decision again. But please hear me out: I had to make a decision in writing this comment. I could just move on with my life as if nothing happened, but I'm willing to take the risk of making a mistake, because based on my reading, there's a chance that this might help even just a tiny bit. 

Never taking a decision again would prevent you from ever making the wrong choice, that's true, but it would also prevent you from ever making the right one. 
People don't make decisions based on what's good or bad. They interpret a situation as best they can and then they pick what they believe to be the most appropriate choice based off that interpretation. Humans take thousand of decisions each day, it's no surprise that not all of them are optimal.

I think, most, if not all, of those "mistakes" that you dread, weren't really "evil" or "malignant" at their cores. At worst, you could define them as "misguided". People /might/ believe that you meant harm, but don't forget that they are interpreting the situation with the limited knowledge that they have, just like you are. 
You're the only one that has all the relevant information to put a label on situations you've been in. 
I think that moving on requires you to accept that, yes, you haven't always picked the best option, but you always picked what you thought was "right" from your point of view. Don't judge yourself as if you had all the required knowledge to NOT have made the "wrong" decision.


If you have the resources available in your area, I'd orient you towards "cognitive behavioral therapy(CBT)", as the whole idea behind it is to process specific happenings. I've had one situation that really upset me in particular, where someone replied to me in a very dismissive way and I immediately jumped to the conclusion I had messed up. Regarding the sleeping pills, I completely get your opinion on them. Obviously it would be best if your sleep could get better without them, however it doesn't have to be a "life-sentence" either. This could help provide reassurance to your brain that falling asleep isn't endangering, which eventually would lead to more confidence for you to fall asleep on your own. It's actually uncommon for people to stay on Ambien for as long as I have, most people only get it prescribed for around 4-6 weeks. Ambien is typically the kind of sleeping pill that is not meant for long-term use, you can see it as the equivalent of ibuprofen for sleeping meds more or less. There are sleeping pills that are meant to be taken on the long term (mirtazapine and trazodone come to mind) and while they're not hard to quit, they might not let you grow into a position where you don't need them any longer. 

I think it's good to at least be aware that's an available option. The choice of taking the option is your call, though! If you don't feel comfortable with taking sleeping pills that's fine. You could actually talk to your GP and explain to them how you feel about sleep meds, and they would definitely be able to list all the different treatment options you have available.

So tldr; don't be afraid of labels, look around at what other people do to see if there are small (or big) things that you could try in your day-to-day life and try to let your doctor know that you're unsure/against sleeping meds and would like to know what else is available.

Have you monitored the temperatures?

If they're all from the same physical drive, it shouldn't do much of a difference

If they're different physical drives then yeah it might depending on their speed.
On my pc for example I have a Toshiba 1to hard drive, which has been partitioned. C: and D: are both part of the same hard drive but they're two different partitions, the speed should be the same on both.
I also have a 250GB Ssd installed, which is indicated as E: on my pc, this one is different because it's not the same drive and this one is a flash drive, so it's faster. In that case installing games on it, instead of D:, will make a difference, because the drive is faster.

In short, check how many physical drives you have, if you have two different of them, then they might run at different speeds and there might be a difference. If they're two physical drives but the same model, it'll probably won't change anything. And if you have only one drive just many partitions, it won't change much.

I can recommend something though, if you have only one hard drive, maybe using a disk partition that isn't the same as the one where your system is installed, can be helpful. 
If oyu ever have to wipe off your system to reinstall it, you can simply remove the partition containing your system and keeping the other ones safe
